title: New Zealand rearguard holds India to draw first Test
text:
Australia have moved up to join leaders and reigning champions South Africa in the 2025-2027 World Test Championship top two after New Zealand and India drew at Basin Reserve in Wellington.

New Zealand fought a battling rearguard on Monday to deny ‌India in the first Test, but drop out of the top two in the WTC standings due to the draw, while India remain in fourth.

The tourists ended five wickets short of converting their mammoth ‌first-innings lead into a victory, after India entered the final day requiring eight dismissals to take a 1-0 lead in the series.

New Zealand were 5-239 in their second innings, still trailing India's first-innings 9-720 declared by 113 runs, when the captains shook hands to end the contest.

Daryl Mitchell and first-innings centurion Glenn Phillips put on 63 for the sixth wicket on a Basin Reserve track that had been all but lifeless since the ‌opening session and a bit of the ‌match.

The pair stayed together for 43 overs, Phillips scoring 26 from 126 balls and Mitchell 49 not out from 186 balls before the teams shook hands and stumps were drawn with an hour remaining in the day.

"As you look back over the five days from that first innings to where the game ended up, the wicket changed throughout but I thought it was a great Test match," Nicholls said.

"Both teams gave it everything.

"For us to get a draw from where we were was a pleasing result."

Daryl Mitchell was not out on 49 when the captains shook hands. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India will take ⁠some confidence from their batting performance heading to Christchurch for the start of the second Test ​on Friday after six players scored half centuries or better in their single, record-breaking innings of 9-720.

KL Rahul and Rishabh Pant both grabbed centuries in contrasting styles, while skipper Shubman Gill fell two runs short of the milestone.

Pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah impressed on his return to Test cricket after a year out as he helped reduce New Zealand to 5-70 on the opening day, although he was used sparingly as India chased the result on Monday.

New Zealand's match was the tale of two sixth-wicket ‌stands.

The first was ​of 216 runs between Henry Nicholls (175 not out) and Phillips (118) that enabled the hosts to post a respectable 368 in their first knock.

The ​second between Phillips ‌and Mitchell on Monday was never going to be about the tally of runs but more about how long they occupied the ​crease.

They came together in the sixth over after lunch when Tom Blundell departed for 15 via DRS review off the bowling of Anshul Kamboj to leave New Zealand at 5-176.

In the opening session, spinner Washington Sundar had made ‌the first breakthrough by removing Devon Conway for 65, after the ball popped up off the opener's bat and pad for Pant to collect with an athletic catch.

Rachin Ravindra, the other overnight batter, followed for 37 with a miscued shot off the bowling of seamer Prasidh Krishna that flew to Rahul in the slips.

India will rue a few missed chances to make further inroads into the New Zealand batting order, most notably ​a potential run out that would have sent Mitchell back early in his innings.

"We knew it was going to be a challenge to get 10 wickets on that pitch," India captain Gill said.

"We had a couple of chances and a decent day in the field. I think we challenged them in all areas."

AAP/AP

title: Jobs cuts will diminish Tasmanian museum, historian says
text:
Four Queen Victoria Museum and Art Gallery (QVMAG) staff with a combined experience of 90 years have been made redundant, as part of a restructure by the City of Launceston.

The Launceston City Council will cut 10 full-time equivalent jobs as it aims to save about $1.9 million a year.

The ABC understands this includes roles in QVMAG's history department, including a senior curator, assistant curator and a technical officer, along with another technical officer from the museum's archives.

Staff at Launceston's Queen Victoria Museum and Art Gallery will be impacted by the redundancies. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Oral History Tasmania President Jill Cassidy told 936 ABC Hobart that as a result of the cuts, there would be no-one left in the history department, aside from one archivist.

"I know just how much the collections of the museum have been bolstered by all those people around Tasmania, but particularly the Launceston area, who expect that their collections will be looked after," Ms Cassidy said.

" The whole museum has been uprooted by the fact that we're going to lose a senior curator in history. "

Jill Cassidy says there is an expectation the public collections would be looked after. (ABC News: Damian McIntyre)

"The council just really needs to look at itself to find out how this could be happening; that so much experience should be booted out the door with no thought of what the future will hold."

Not everything is digitised

Launceston historian John Dent said while the museum's online portal was useful, local historians would still need to access information through staff.

"A lot of the information isn't digitised," Mr Dent said.

"So it's necessary to talk to the people and the staff at QVMAG to be able to get access to a lot of this information that they have such an extensive collective 90 years experience in.

"It's going to diminish the accessibility of the collection and it's going to be much harder and more difficult for [remaining] staff to respond.

"You cut culture, you don't see the value that it adds to our community. But these cultural institutions, it's what we are."

John Dent says the staff cuts to the QVMAG will "diminish the accessibility of the collection". (ABC News: Damian McIntyre)

Earlier in November, the council said in a statement it was changing its "organisational structure" and was working with the affected employees.

"The changes made are expected to deliver significant operational savings without compromising service delivery," it said.

The council was contacted for further comment.

TMAG cuts to be tabled

The Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery has nearly a million items from the state collection in its care. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Jobs at Tasmania's state-owned museum the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG) are also in question.

Tasmanian museum facing staff cuts Staff at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG) say that nearly 20 full-time-equivalent jobs are on the chopping block, equating to about 30 per cent of the institution's workforce.

In August, staff at TMAG said they were informed nearly 20 jobs were due to be cut.

The state government said the claims were false, but conceded there would be job cuts across the department overseeing TMAG, including at the gallery.

Independent Member for Nelson Meg Webb is raising a motion in parliament's Upper House this week calling on the government to reverse the decision.

"I am hopeful my upper house colleagues will see fit this week to add their voices to those local, national and international calls for an urgent rethink and reversal of these funding cuts," Ms Webb said.

title: Devastating injury blow for Adams days after making Socceroos debut
text:
New Socceroo Eli Adams faces nearly a year on the sidelines through a horror knee injury.

Adams made his first appearance for Australia off the bench in last week's 3-0 friendly win over Qatar, but was injured at training and had to leave camp before the Socceroos' 2-0 loss to Jordan.

His Japanese club Gamba Osaka confirmed today that Adams had ruptured the ACL in his left knee, along with injuring his MCL and suffering a lateral meniscus tear.

The 24-year-old will return to Australia to start his rehabilitation.

The Queenslander will have a knee reconstruction and faces at least several months — if not up to a year — on the sidelines.

It is a shocking blow for Adams, who earned a move to Japan off the back of stellar form at the Newcastle Jets.

Between 2024 and 2026, Adams scored 20 goals in 52 A-League appearances for Newcastle.

He has since notched two goals in 15 appearances for Gamba Osaka.

AAP

title: Jim Chalmers says he doesn't expect a recession, but 'things might get a bit harder'
text:
Next year will see more jobs lost and households cut back their spending, but Treasurer Jim Chalmers says a recession is not forecast despite the prospect that 'things might get a bit harder' in 2027.

Providing an update on the state of the economy on Monday, Mr Chalmers said he would deliver substantial spending cuts in next month's update to the budget, and that these cuts were likely to more than cover any new spending.

"We know that no realistic amount of savings makes inflation go away, but too much new spending can make it worse," the treasurer told the parliament. It is some of his most direct language to date about the link between the budget and inflation.

"We understand and embrace our role in the fight against inflation… Cutting spending enough, without threatening growth," he said.

The mid-year budget update will also include an update to Treasury's forecasts for the economy. Mr Chalmers said that as things stood, unemployment would hit a peak above 5 per cent, compared to the 4.5 per cent forecast at budget.

The growth forecast would be "well below" 2 per cent for the next two years and inflation would not return to within the Reserve Bank's 2-3 per cent target band until the end of 2027.

Mr Chalmers said it was "not yet clear" how five interest rate hikes this year would affect the economy but that "the risks are substantial" that they could worsen the situation in the job market, the housing market and the broader economy.

"We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier," he said.

Don't expect further cost of living relief

The government has been weighed down by gloomy economic conditions, with interest rates now at their highest level since 2008 and unemployment reaching a six-year high.

The Opposition Leader Angus Taylor used Question Time to call for the treasurer to be sacked, saying he "can't manage money" and that "Australia is on a road to economic ruin" under his stewardship.

Mr Chalmers accused the Coalition of hypocrisy for opposing savings measures currently before the Senate, including a reduction to the private health insurance rebate given to older Australians.

Cuts to government spending coming Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirms a "substantial" package of savings in the mid-year budget update, which will be delivered in December.

"They say it's about spending, then they vote against budget repair in the Senate… They say it's about confidence and then they talk our economy down at every turn," he said.

The government announced today that it would freeze PBS medicine scripts at $25 each until the end of the decade, in a bid to win support from the Greens or the Coalition for the private health cut.

Mr Chalmers suggested this additional cost-of-living measure would not be followed by many others. "There's no responsible amount of cost-of-living assistance that would make the impact of cumulative price rises go away entirely," he said.

Beyond saying that cuts would spare essential services and would not be "concentrated in one area or portfolio," Mr Chalmers gave few details about specifics.

But he said there were other factors worsening the budget. A weaker economy and high inflation would mean lower tax collection overall in the next four years, and more spending on existing government programs.

"It would not be responsible to fully offset these big changes… We expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on," he said.

The treasurer identified some bright spots, saying the mid-year budget would again forecast wages growing faster than prices, and that business investment was set to grow twice as fast this year as to what was forecast in the budget.

"So much of the daily commentary on our economy is stuck in an endless spiral of negativity designed to be a self-fulfilling prophecy. The outlook is uncertain but a recovery in real wages in 2027 will partly ease some of these pressures," he said.

title: TV star Matt Wright pleads guilty to failing helicopter maintenance duties
text:
Television star and celebrity crocodile wrangler Matt Wright has pleaded guilty to failing to maintain his helicopters, exposing pilots and passengers to a "serious risk of injury or death".

Wright faced the Darwin Local Court today where he pleaded guilty to a single count of breaching his duties as a director of chopper company Helibrook between September 2021 and November 2022.

Helibrook was also facing charges under work safety laws, however they were withdrawn due to the company going into liquidation.

Matt Wright arrived at court this morning with defence barrister Lyma Nguyen before entering a guilty plea. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

The court heard Wright failed to ensure the flying hours of three choppers operated by his company were accurately recorded and failed to comply with maintenance requirements.

According to agreed facts read in court, Wright "exposed himself and other pilots to a serious risk of injury or death" including a risk of "mid-flight engine failure".

Loading...

Conduct motivated by 'commercial benefit'

Prosecutor Nicholas Goodfellow described Wright's conduct as "deliberate" and "sustained", saying it was designed to "prolong maintenance".

"There was a commercial benefit that underpinned or flowed from this activity," he said.

" The steps required to comply were simple — they were simply to record the hours. "

Mr Goodfellow said the recording of flight hours was "fundamental" to aircraft safety and deterring the practice by others in the aviation industry should be a significant factor for the court.

Nicholas Goodfellow said the recording of flight hours was "fundamental" to aircraft safety. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"It is critical a message is sent … that they must record hours accurately," he said.

Tampering about 'convenience'

The court heard Hobbs meters, which record flying hours, on Wright's helicopters were disabled, preventing the data from being accurately recorded.

Wright's barrister Lyma Nguyen argued his conduct was motivated by "convenience", not financial gain.

"Mr Wright was willing and did indeed spend a lot of money on maintaining his helicopters," she said.

Judge Stephen Geary challenged that submission, questioning what motivation he could have had other than financial gain.

The court heard "intense" publicity had "destroyed [Wright's] reputation and his businesses". (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"Mr Wright knowingly engaged in disconnecting the Hobbs meter on his helicopters to prevent flying hours from being accurately recorded," he said.

"You only do that to keep it in the air … to save money."

Ms Nguyen said Wright's conduct could be equated to tampering with an odometer on a car.

But Judge Geary said "you can't compare it to a car".

"A car, when they break down, they stop.

" But a helicopter … the risk is it's up there, the engine stops and it doesn't glide down, does it? "

Prison release 'revoked' by faulty warrant

Ms Nguyen said her client had already suffered additional forms of "punishment" including "unrelenting" media scrutiny and "financial woes".

Ms Nguyen said Wright and his family had faced "intense" publicity, much of which she described as "unfair and inaccurate".

"This has destroyed his reputation and his businesses," she said.

Lyma Nguyen compared Wright's conduct to tampering with a car's odometer. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

Ms Nguyen tendered a psychological report and said Wright had been diagnosed with "complex PTSD", "arising out of some chronic stresses … including the way the media have handled this matter".

Wright was released from prison in May after serving five months following a lengthy criminal trial last year on separate charges of attempting to pervert the course of justice.

On Monday, Ms Nguyen told the court while Wright was serving his sentence, a warrant was "incorrectly issued" for his work safety charges, resulting in an order for his early release on home detention being revoked.

"For whatever reason, the commissioner of corrections chose not to reinstate the administrative home detention permit which he would have been on if it were not for the incorrectly issued warrant," she said.

Matt Wright blamed the corrections commissioner for the fact he missed the birth of his baby. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

Ms Nguyen said her client had "effectively" served an additional month in custody, resulting in him missing the birth of his third child, with the mistake the subject of a complaint to the ombudsman.

Judge Geary said while the decision to revoke his early release might have been "terribly unfair", it could not be considered "unlawful" without evidence.

Speaking outside court, Wright said he blamed the commissioner for missing the birth of his baby.

"There were three occasions he put a stop to my home detention which was pretty rough on the family," he said.

Wright confirmed he had lodged a complaint with the ombudsman.

Lyma Nguyen said a warrant was "incorrectly issued" for Wright's work safety charges. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"I want to know why," he said.

"Why did he hold me back when so many other people get let out on home [detention].

"The impact on the family was huge."

Ms Nguyen said the court should take into account Wright's "exemplary character" and his contribution to the community through tourism and charity work.

"He has made extraordinary contributions to the profile of NT tourism," she said.

Lyma Nguyen tendered a character reference for Wright from country music star Lee Kernaghan. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

Ms Nguyen tendered several character references in support of Wright including from country music singer Lee Kernaghan, Wright's agent Nick Fordham and high-profile crocodile farmer Mick Burns.

Judge Geary will hand down his sentence on December 22.

title: Supreme Court dismisses residents' MotoGP challenge
text:
The Malinauskas government's MotoGP circuit in the eastern parklands has cleared another hurdle, with the Supreme Court dismissing a resident group's legal bid to halt the redevelopment.

The legal challenge, lodged in October by the South East City Residents Association (SECRA), sought to halt the $96 million circuit redevelopment on the basis that the state's motorsport legislation did not grant the South Australian Motor Sport Board the power to remove trees.

But Supreme Court Justice Katrina Bochner dismissed the application during a brief hearing on Monday.

In her reasons published after the hearing, Justice Bochner said it was not the court's role to determine "whether it is desirable to hold the MotoGP within the city of Adelaide, nor whether it is undesirable that trees be felled … to facilitate the holding of the MotoGP".

"The only role that this Court has is to determine whether the removal of trees by the Board within the declared area specified by the Minister is authorised by the Act," she said in her reasons.

The justice said the South Australian Motor Sport Act 1984 "confers on the Board the power to remove trees from parklands (including the Adelaide Park Lands), if their removal is reasonably necessary for or incidental to the performance of its functions".

Protesters oppose the removal of trees for the MotoGP circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Residents intend to continue legal pursuit of government

Outside court after the hearing, SECRA committee spokesperson Wilfrid Prest said the ruling meant the Motor Sport Board had "extraordinarily broad" powers.

"They're really unfettered powers, almost, you might say, autocratic powers," said Mr Prest.

He said the association had accepted the justice's ruling but would explore what other legal avenues were available to challenge the project.

"The game isn't over, or the fight isn't over, we will certainly be looking very closely at the reasons that have been stated by her honour, and we will be considering the possibility of an appeal," he said.

" There may also be other legal avenues that we will look to follow. "

SECRA has called on the government "not to proceed with a project which threatens irreparable environmental damage at considerable expense and to doubtful economic benefit".

Mr Prest said results of a poll recently conducted by the group would be released tomorrow.

He said those results showed "many thousands of South Australians have opposition [to the circuit]".

Wilfred Prest said SECRA would explore its legal options after its case was dismissed. (ABC News)

Works set to commence in December

The government's legal victory over SECRA comes after an earlier Federal Court challenge to the circuit lodged by Queensland man Joshua Hogan was withdrawn.

The Federal Court also ruled against a separate legal challenge lodged by public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna woman Janette Milera against the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade, which required felling 585 trees.

Premier Peter Malinauskas said he welcomed today's Supreme Court decision.

"[The decision] simply confirms that the state government has acted lawfully and prudently and thoughtfully as we sought to craft our policy for the upgrade of the street circuit and the parklands," he said.

Mr Malinauskas said unlike previous challenges brought before the court, the government had indicated it would pursue full legal costs for the failed litigation.

Peter Malinauskas welcomed the court's decision on Monday. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"In regards to this particular matter, it being funded by a range of individuals through an organisation," he said.

" We will absolutely be pressing for full costs. "

The judgement follows an expedited, one-day hearing on November 17, where the court heard arguments from both SECRA and the government about the powers granted under the Motor Sport Act.

Construction on the new circuit is officially due to begin in December ahead of the first MotoGP event in Adelaide in November 2027.

A total of 377 trees, 42 classed as significant, are slated for destruction to make way for the $96 million circuit.

Seven trees have already been removed to allow works on utility infrastructure.

The government has promised to replace the trees at a 10-to-1 ratio.

title: Geoff Henke, Winter Olympics 'dream maker', dies aged 99
text:
The sporting world is littered with legends.

Few have done more to earn that label than Geoff Henke, who died on Sunday in Melbourne. He was 99.

To describe Henke as a visionary sports administrator would barely scratch the surface of what he achieved on behalf of Australia's elite snow and ice athletes.

"Geoff Henke was the founding father of Australian winter sport," Australian Olympic Committee (AOC) president Ian Chesterman said in a statement.

"Every winter sport Australian athlete has benefited from Geoff's vision, his persistence, and his refusal to accept that winter sport did not have a place in this country.

"Geoff gave his life to winter sport and to the Olympic Movement.

"He fought for winter athletes at a time when few others would and never stopped.

"He saw what Australian winter athletes could achieve long before anyone else did, and he spent decades making sure they had the chance to prove it."

Henke, an Australian ice hockey representative for 13 years, was denied the chance to compete at an Olympic Games himself.

The 70-year-old snub that put Australia on the path to Winter Olympics glory Geoff Henke was denied a chance to compete at the 1956 Cortina Olympics. That snubbing led to a lifetime of advocacy for Winter Sports, leading to the 2026 Games at the same venue.

In 1956, the Australian team that he was a part of was set to head to Cortina to take part in the Games, only for the then-chairman of the AOC to refuse to sanction them.

Four years later, Henke did not travel to Squaw Valley, a decision he told ABC Sport he regretted.

But it was his snubbing that meant Henke would fight tooth and nail to ensure that everyone who had a chance to compete at a Games could.

He served as Australia's Chef de Mission at six consecutive Winter Olympic Games, starting in Innsbruck in 1976 and going right through to Lillehammer 1994.

At that 1994 Olympics, Australia won its first ever Winter Olympic medal, a bronze in the men’s 5,000m short track speed skating relay.

The nation has won at least one medal at every Winter Olympic Games since, culminating in the stunning, record-breaking performance in Milan-Cortina earlier this year.

While so many people at those Games wondered how a sun-burned country such as Australia could ever compete on the same level as established Winter Olympic powerhouses, the answers could find their root cause with one name: Geoff Henke.

Geoff Henke (middle in suit), stands at at the Brisbane Water Ramp, next to future Olympic silver medallist Dani Scott. (Getty Images: Jono Searle)

"Geoff was a dream maker," Milano-Cortina Chef de Mission and two-time Olympic medallist Alisa Camplin said.

"He always had a sparkle in his eye and a project on the go — his belief in what Australia's winter athletes could deliver was unparalleled."

Henke, who was inducted into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame, was instrumental in the establishment of a high-performance centre for Australian skiing at Mount Buller, which helped Zali Steggall to bronze at the 1998 Nagano Olympics, Australia's only Olympic medal to date in Alpine skiing.

He then went on to establish the Olympic Winter Institute of Australia in 1998, and served as its chairperson for 24 years.

During those 24 years under his stewardship, Australia won 17 Olympic medals, 16 World Championship titles, 38 World Championship medals and 364 World Cup medals.

Henke's staunch and repeated advocacy resulted in the building of the water ramp in Brisbane, which opened in 2021, something Henke described as a "miracle".

Twelve of Australia's 2026 Winter Olympians train there, and four of the record-breaking six Olympic medals were won by those athletes, including gold medals to Jakara Anthony and Cooper Woods.

The Geoff Henke Winter Olympic training centre is a lasting legacy. (ABC Sport: Simon Smale)

Henke was also a huge advocate for the Ice House in his home town of Melbourne, with its main competition rink named after him.

"Winter athletes of the last 30 years profusely thank Geoff for setting up the engine room that's enabled our Winter Olympic dreams to come true," Camplin said.

"Geoff's legacy goes beyond the results we enjoyed in Milano Cortina early this year. He showed us how to live a passionate and purposeful life, and how important it is to give back to the winter community and our country."

Henke's joy at the development in winter sport was evident to anyone who spoke to him.

Even this past weekend, it is said he was deeply enthused by the top-10 World Cup finish of slalom skier Madi Hoffman.

"Every winter sport Australian athlete who competes at the Olympic Winter Games today does so from the foundations he built," Chesterman said.

"His legacy is measured not only in medals Australia has won, but in the sport systems he built, the facilities and opportunities that exist today for young Australians who dream of competing at the Winter Games.

"Personally, Geoff started as my boss, became my mentor and we finished as the greatest of friends. Geoff was loved and admired by many and will be sadly missed."

Henke is survived by his wife, Gweneth, and their daughter, Joanne, both of whom are Winter Olympians.

title: Integrity watchdog's secret report could be made public after legal fix
text:
Legislative amendments will be introduced to Tasmania's parliament this week to ensure the state's integrity commission can publish its own tribunal reports, deputy premier Guy Barnett has said.

The Integrity Commission confirmed to the ABC last week that its powers to table the final report into Investigation Cuvier in parliament were "unclear".

Cuvier, which relates to allegations of misconduct in the public service, is the watchdog's first and only tribunal hearing, and took six years.

Under Tasmania's laws, a tribunal can decide to publish its findings, but the commission has legal advice that determines whether a tribunal ceases to exist after it provides its report to involved parties.

Guy Barnett said the issue with tabling investigative reports had only "emerged very recently" and that more consideration was needed. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Barnett told parliament's Joint Standing Committee on Integrity that his office was working on a legislative amendment, "with the aim of having this amendment ready to introduce when the Integrity Commission Amendment Bill 2026 is debated in the house this week".

The Integrity Commission Amendment Bill 2026 implements some reforms recommended by William Cox's 2016 review.

Chief Commissioner Robert Hay told the committee it was a "huge issue" that the commission could not table its own reports, saying "we need to have that power".

Mr Hay said the court had made the ruling based on Section 11.4 of the act, which gives the commission the power to table reports.

"The court effectively found that those provisions restrict the commission's ability to provide reports or make reports to our administrative functions," he said.

"Or how we perform our functions, as opposed to telling you about details of an investigation or the results of an investigation."

Mr Barnett said the legislative amendments will be introduced to Tasmania's parliament this week. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Issue of secrecy emerged only 'recently'

In a hearing last week, Hobart barrister Chris Gunson told the committee the Supreme Court had recently ruled the commission also did not have the power to table investigative reports.

Integrity reports remain secret amid 'unclear' rules on release A senior lawyer says Tasmania's Integrity Commission does not have the power to table its investigations in parliament.

Mr Gunson has been involved in multiple integrity commission matters, including Operation Cuvier.

He also represented MP Madeleine Ogilvie in Investigation Loyatea, which related to 2021 Liberal Party state election grants.

Mr Barnett said the issue with tabling investigative reports had only "emerged very recently" and that more consideration was needed.

He added that he had not seen the court's decision, as it was suppressed.

In his hearing, Mr Gunson suggested that reports be given to the Joint Standing Committee on Integrity, for it publish.

Mr Barnett said he was seeking advice on the matter, but Mr Hay said he did not believe the act allowed it to be done.

Commission calls for 'public interest test'

The commission's confidentiality rules have also been criticised, as government MPs are unable to answer questions about investigations.

Loading...

Last week, Mr Gunson told the committee that the commission implements confidentiality "as a matter of course", despite having discretion.

Integrity Commission chief executive Ellen McKenzie said confidentiality rules were used to "preserve the integrity of the matter" and to ensure there was "no interference with evidence or witnesses".

"I accept, of course, that it becomes difficult in terms of the continuation of those confidentiality requirements if a matter becomes elongated due to whatever the issue is," she said.

Ms McKenzie suggested a "public interest test or reasonable cause test" be added to the act.

The commission has recommended the act provide "clear, efficient and expedited mechanisms" to resolve legal challenges.

Mr Hay said litigation was a key hold up.

"If you attack an investigation, that stops the investigation," he said.

"If you attack something before the board tables a report with parliament, that stops the report being tabled in parliament until the matter is heard and determined.

"We get attacked a lot for delays, but litigation has a major effect years at times on delays."

title: News account only disclosed it was authorised by LNP after ABC questions
text:
A social media account promoting itself as a Queensland news source only disclosed it was authorised by the Liberal National Party following questions from the ABC.

This month Queensland Breaking News started sharing Instagram reels from government press conferences spruiking announcements made by ministers.

Its posts on transport and infrastructure projects have been re-posted by Premier David Crisafulli and Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, with its best performing content reaching almost 10,000 views.

The account's maroon and white logo featuring a map of Queensland is in stark contrast to LNP's trademark blue.

Following questions to the government from the ABC an authorisation statement was added to the account's bio to appear alongside its tagline "latest updates from across QLD".

An LNP spokesperson said: "Queensland Breaking News is one of many pages used by the LNP to share information about what the LNP Government is delivering for Queensland."

An authorisation was added to the bio for the Queensland Breaking News Instagram account after questions from the ABC. (Supplied: Instagram)

While an authorisation was added, it is not a legal requirement. In Queensland, authorisation of election material, including social media accounts, is only required 12 months before a state election.

For the next state election in 2028, this will apply from October next year.

The Electoral Commission of Queensland does not regulate authorisation of election matter outside of the authorisation period.

It is among a string of politically linked accounts promoting themselves as news sources at both a state and federal level.

Queensland Politics Newsfeed, which is authorised by Queensland's Labor opposition, has been active since 2024 when the party was in office.

It posts reels from press conferences, with Opposition Leader Steven Miles prominently featured and uses the hashtag #qldupdates.

Across the border, an Instagram account with the handle @nswnewsroom states that it is authorised by the Labor Party. According to the Sydney Morning Herald, this detail was added after the government was approached for comment.

NSW Labor's 'newsroom' social media account raises a political eyebrow From a "breaking" news-style post about the gun buyback scheme to a video of jacarandas blooming, the scribes behind the social media account have been busy.

Australian National University marketing lecturer Dr Andrew Hughes said the accounts "purport" to be reporting on the news but only tell one side of the story.

"They are growing in popularity in use because they fall outside a hard definition of being election material which would then have to be authorised," he said.

"It is attractive to a party because it might take some time for someone, like a normal person, to deduct that is being done by a party."

The Instagram page posts press conferences from LNP politicians in Queensland. (Instagram: @qldbreakingnews)

Dr Hughes said political advertising laws should be changed to require the authorisation of content at all times to reflect the changing media landscape and strategies used to reach voters.

"In the age of digital and social media, it is ongoing, it does not stop," he said.

Dr Hughes said including an authorisation on an account allows a political party to say they are not hiding who they are and where the information is coming from.

"In the modern age of social media, you don't want to go for paid; you want to get the viral effect, which is it is shared by people among their networks," he said.

title: Cricket NSW slams door on Bears' North Sydney NRL homecoming
text:
Cricket NSW has slammed the door on a Bears NRL pre-season homecoming, ruling out making North Sydney Oval available for Perth to play at in February.

Cricket officials informed the Bears today that they would not accept any financial compensation for use of the venue, given it would remove cricket for at least five weeks.

It comes after NRL executive chair Peter V'landys last week said it would be "beyond comprehension" for cricket to deny the expansion club a romantic homecoming.

V'landys also claimed a $200,000 compensation fee would be "silly", after Cricket NSW indicated that would be the cost to take the pitch out and put it back in.

The Bears will play in the NRL in 2027. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But Cricket NSW chief executive Lee Germon said ultimately, money was not a factor, and instead his sport had to look after the North Sydney Cricket Club and stop them being moved for four games.

"It became very evident the impact to cricket was too great to agree to this request," Germon said.

"North Sydney have been playing at North Sydney Oval since 1895, so it is very much a key home and a spiritual home for them as well.

"We want them to play as much cricket as we can there.

"But because it is such a great cricket ground we have WBBL and international women's matches there as well, which also restricts accessibility for the club."

Bears unlikely to be able to play at oval in future

Germon warned it was unlikely cricket would be moved out of North Sydney in the future for the Bears due to the annual schedule.

That would leave Perth never able to play at the Bears' spiritual home, given North Sydney is unlikely to be considered fit for a regular-season NRL match.

"It's a key cricket ground," Germon said.

"We are faced with this every year. We would love to host a Sheffield Shield final at the SCG, but we can't because of the AFL.

Can the Bears live between North Sydney Oval and Perth? North Sydney Oval kept the spirit of the Bears alive during their darkest hours. But what role can the famous old ground play in the foundation club's resurrection in Perth?

"It's the world we live in. Cricket has the rights to North Sydney Oval in cricket season, and cricket is a summer sport.

"So it's very unlikely we would be able to accommodate any request of this nature, moving forward."

Germon said he had some sympathy for the Bears, who are scheduled to play their first pre-season match at the little-known western Sydney ground, Eric Tweedale Stadium.

But asked how he thought V'landys may feel about the situation, Germon said he was not fussed.

"I don't know, I don't know him. And I don't really care," he quipped.

"It's a decision we have made and it is a decision in the best interest of our sport."

title: Sydney Opera House disabled access changes unsafe, some patrons say
text:
Sydney Opera House patrons and some staff have slammed changes to the building's disabled access, which they claim are unsafe and were made without proper consultation.

Accessible drop-off at the Opera House has been moved from the underground loading dock to the main arrival area at the Macquarie Street Gatehouse.

Patrons requiring assistance are now picked up from the gatehouse by golf buggies and driven to the door.

Barbara Hutchinson said the new arrangements were difficult to navigate for her and her friend, Jane Stone, who uses two walking sticks and has difficulty walking long distances.

"[Before] we were able to access the loading dock, and they allowed taxis to go down and unload people and they were beautifully helpful," Ms Hutchinson told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings.

"They had wheelchairs and walkers, all sorts of things. But we went on Tuesday night and we were told that's no longer available.

"It does make it very difficult for people who are very disabled and in a wheelchair."

Ms Stone said she was able to safely navigate the new buggy system but that some disabled people would struggle.

"The distance between the front of the [buggy] seat and the back of the seat in front is very small," she said.

The Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) sent an open letter on October 29 on behalf of staff to Sydney Opera House management which detailed safety concerns with the new buggy system.

The union said it was yet to receive a formal response.

MEAA acting chief executive Adam Portelli said there had been two incidents in which staff and a patron were injured while travelling in the buggies.

"Patrons who previously were able to enter or leave from the venue directly now need to get dropped off and picked up 150 metres away, brave the elements, and then get a buggy into the Opera House," Mr Portelli said.

"The buggy itself … presents a real OHS risk."

In a statement, a Sydney Opera House spokesperson said the change removed the need for visitors to use back-of-house pathways, mitigating the safety risks of moving through a working loading dock while consolidating all visitor arrivals in one location.

It said there were three enclosed buggies for transporting visitors between the arrival area and the building, two of which were fitted with ramps for wheelchair users.

"The Opera House is committed to delivering the highest standard of customer service, inclusivity and patron safety," they said.

David, an Elizabeth Bay resident, said he had been visiting the Opera House since it opened in 1973.

He said the change was made without any warning.

"It's just appalling," he said.

"[Visitors] were essentially told to get out of the car and to get into a buggy. And when you're an older person without the ability to put any weight, any strength, one step is one step too far," he said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese joined Kylie Minogue, Jimmy Barnes and Blondie in paying tribute to Australian music legend Ian “Molly” Meldrum following his death at the age of 83. As the host of Countdown, Meldrum brought local and international music to our television screens in a must-watch program the likes of which this country had never seen. With an often bumbling, loose interviewing style, he won the hearts of viewers and artists alike. Molly Meldrum has died aged 83. He had long been ill and died at 5.30am on Monday at the Epworth Hospital in Richmond, in inner Melbourne. He will be granted a state funeral. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Australian music legend, journalist, producer and cultural icon Ian Alexander ‘Molly’ Meldrum AM … He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him,” his family said via a statement.

Advertisement

“Affectionately dubbed ‘The Guru’, Meldrum was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music. He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them … He lived and breathed music, believing in its power to unite, to inspire and to lift up young musicians.” In 1974, Meldrum helped develop Countdown, working as a talent co-ordinator, interviewer and presenter on the show. His catchphrase “Do yourself a favour” entered the Australian vernacular. Loading On the show, he championed acts like AC/DC and Russell Morris and brought international icons including Elton John, ABBA and Madonna to Australian audiences. After Countdown ended, Meldrum joined Hey Hey It’s Saturday, hosting the music and entertainment segment Molly’s Melodrama. He also hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid (Oz for Africa ) in 1985.

Advertisement

Gavin Wood, who worked with Meldrum on Countdown, described his friend and former colleague as “one of the craziest, most colourful, funniest and most beautiful people you could ever have the pleasure of meeting”. ‘There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him.’ Gavin Wood “He was absolutely one of a kind, and it was a privilege to know him,” Wood wrote on Facebook. “What he has done for the Australian music industry is simply phenomenal. His contribution, passion, enthusiasm and unwavering commitment to Australian artists helped shape an entire generation of music and entertainment. “There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him. He was an original, a trailblazer and a true institution of Australian entertainment. Fly high my friend.”

Advertisement

Kylie Minogue posted that she would turn up the music in his honour. “As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room and dreaming of how music might become part of my life,” she wrote. Floral tributes were placed outside Meldrum’s home in the Melbourne suburb of Richmond on Monday following news of his death. Simon Schluter Jimmy Barnes said on Instagram that the impact of appearing on Countdown was immediate. “Our shows went from pubs to bigger pubs to big halls in a matter of months. Molly exposed us to a huge music audience we could never have reached and we were always thankful to him for that.” In a tribute posted to X, the prime minister said Meldrum “loved music almost as much as we loved him”.

Advertisement

“He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace. And over the years ... he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him,” Albanese wrote. Singer Marcia Hines thanked Meldrum for “everything that he did for us all in the Australian music industry and worldwide” in a tribute on Facebook. Loading Australian Crawl frontman James Reyne said Meldrum’s support on the must-watch Countdown launch the band. “He was very important at that period for Australian music,” Reyne said. “Countdown was such a great platform to expose people to it.” Singer Kate Ceberano described Meldrum as “the fan all artists wish to have”. “They don’t make ’em like that any more. My heart is aching today at the loss.”

Advertisement

Federal Arts Minister Tony Burke, meanwhile, said the country had lost an icon. “For generations of Australians, Molly was more than a familiar face on our television screens. He was an advocate of Australian music, talent scout, journalist, producer and broadcaster who helped shape the soundtrack of our nation,” he said. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said Meldrum’s family had asked for a state funeral and that he would honour that wish. He described Meldrum as “a giant of the Australian music industry and a true character”. Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson paid her respects in a statement, saying that “Australia has lost a legend, and Victoria has lost one of its favourite sons”. On Instagram, Frontier Touring said: “Molly was an original, a passionate advocate for artists and a larger-than-life presence who helped introduce generations of Australians to the music they love”, while promoter Paul Dainty said Meldrum’s contribution to music was immeasurable.

Advertisement

Related Article Vale What Molly Meldrum revealed when I had lunch with him “He championed artists, broke new ground, brought music into people’s homes and lives, and gave generations of musicians a platform and an audience. His influence reached far beyond Australia, and his legacy will live on through the artists he supported and the millions of people he inspired.” American band Blondie shared their sadness at the news, saying, “Molly was instrumental in Blondie’s success in Australia, championing our music and introducing us to a whole new audience. We will always be grateful for his belief in us and the doors he helped open.” Meldrum had lived with an acquired brain injury, the result of a fall from the roof of a pool house at his home in 2011 that left him in an induced coma for weeks. He was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1986, and was the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame, in 2014.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has pledged to produce “budget-sized” spending cuts to put downward pressure on inflation after revealing a bleak economic outlook far worse than expected, with unemployment on track to breach 5 per cent. As economists rate the chances of a local recession at up to fifty-fifty, Chalmers used an address to parliament to warn that the country faced “difficult times full of serious risks”, with economic growth to slip below 2 per cent for the next two years. Jim Chalmers is preparing Australians for a tough economic year ahead. Renee Nowytarger Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese have been under fire over the state of both the economy and the budget, with inflation at 4.3 per cent, unemployment at a five-year-high and real wages falling – all while the budget is in deficit. The Reserve Bank has pushed official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, although financial markets now believe it will have to start cutting by September to help prop up the economy.

Advertisement

Chalmers conceded the economy faced strong headwinds that households were already starting to feel. He said higher oil prices meant inflation was now likely to remain in the mid-threes until near the end of next year. Interest rates would also weigh on household spending. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “This means GDP growth could slow from 2.3 per cent last year to well below 2 per cent for the next two years. Treasury expects unemployment to stay below pre-pandemic averages but now peak higher, above 5 per cent,” he said. “2026 has been a very tough year for our people, our economy and the world. No use pretending otherwise. Interest rates are biting, unemployment is rising, prices are going up, wages aren’t keeping pace and families are hurting.” All forecasts are worse than what Chalmers announced in his May budget. At the time, he forecast economic growth would slow to 1.75 per cent this year before recovering to 2.25 per cent in 2027-28, that inflation would average 2.5 per cent, and that the jobless rate would remain around 4.5 per cent.

Advertisement

Economists with NAB on Monday said the outlook for the jobs market could be even worse, forecasting unemployment to reach 5.5 per cent early in 2028. At that level, the jobless rate would be at its highest level – outside of the pandemic – since 2018. In May, Chalmers forecast the budget would show a deficit of $31.5 billion this financial year, followed by shortfalls of $31 billion, $34.4 billion and $25.3 billion in the three following years. Tax as a share of the economy was forecast to reach 23.8 per cent, its highest point since the 2005-06 record of 24.2 per cent. Government spending as a share of the economy was expected to reach 26.8 per cent. Chalmers said in the short-term the budget deficit was likely to be a little smaller this year but deficits would likely be larger from 2027-28 onwards. The economy is already a little smaller than anticipated, which meant tax and spending as a share of GDP were likely to be slightly higher, even with savings in the mid-year update.

Advertisement

The treasurer said those savings would be spread across the budget, although he argued the government would not slash expenditure. Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market “At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on. We understand and embrace our role in the fight against inflation. Our decisions will deliver a modest net saving despite all these pressures,” he said. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused Chalmers of overseeing a deliberate policy of inflation and policy shock that was undermining confidence among businesses and households. “The prime minister and the treasurer have become the Thelma and Louise of the Australian economy, driving small business and jobs and opportunity off a cliff,” he said.

Advertisement

That cliff could be a domestic recession. HSBC Australia chief economist Paul Bloxham said the deterioration in the economy, particularly in the housing market, meant the chances of the economy going backwards were little better than a coin flip. “We forecast that growth will stall in the coming quarters and see a fifty-fifty chance of a recession,” he said. Bloxham said the AI boom and its call on global savings, on top of the war against Iran, meant interest rates around the world were likely to remain persistently higher than they were before the pandemic. Those higher interest rates are already hitting the budget. Chalmers revealed that if interest on Australian government bonds had remained at 5.4 per cent, a level they reached in early October, then the nation’s interest bill would be $40 billion higher over the next decade.

Advertisement

Loading Bloxham said the government’s changes to housing taxes meant first home buyers were likely to enter a more affordable property market next year. “First home buyers are likely to return to the market more fervently when there are signs the housing price downswing is bottoming, but with fewer investors the eventual upswing is likely to be more subdued than in the past,” he said. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said while the chances of a recession were high, the strength of the AI construction boom and the global economy, plus a recent dip in the Australian dollar, would help support local activity. “However, we would put the risk of recession at a high, and still rising at 40 per cent,” he said.

Advertisement

“The rising trend in unemployment and other indicators of a rising risk of recession are consistent with rate hikes working to slow demand, which will ultimately slow inflation.” The tough outlook was confirmed in S&P’s measure of manufacturing activity, which through November showed the largest fall in business activity in five years. The measure revealed a drop in employment and a broad reduction in new orders. Inflation pressures also fell. “The latest decline in demand reflected the impact of higher interest rates, while softening domestic and external conditions also contributed,” said Jingyi Pan, S&P Global Market Intelligence associate director. The Australian sharemarket trod cautiously on Monday amid rising uneasiness about the outlook for the economy, having last week suffered its worst weekly fall in six years when artificial intelligence anxiety sparked a sell-off in mining and tech stocks. The S&P/ASX 200 slipped 22 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8570.60, with nine of its 11 industry sectors in the red. Miners were a bright spot, as dip buyers waded in after the sector’s sharp losses last week. The Australian dollar was trading at US66.38¢. “We would put the risk of recession at a high and still rising 40 per cent,” Oliver wrote in a research note on Monday, pointing to softening home prices, deteriorating consumer and business sentiment, rising anecdotes of mortgage stress, more job cuts and increasing corporate failures. Queensland politicians are blaming each other for the crisis engulfing the state’s healthcare system, as paramedics say their concerns are not being taken seriously, and frontline workers report being too afraid of losing their jobs to speak out. Seven people have died while waiting for an ambulance since late June, including one Thornlands man who died during an 18-hour wait after calling Triple Zero. Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington was grilled over the pressures facing the system on Monday, as reporters asked why Health Minister Tim Nicholls had not faced media. After an emergency meeting with the premier, Queensland Health director-general and QAS commissioner on Wednesday, he briefly addressed media on Thursday afternoon, holding a prop folder labelled “Labor’s hospital failures”. “I think that the community can have confidence in Triple Zero, and they can have confidence in the paramedics and … the system,” he said.

“Because we’ve got a plan. We’re not dodging responsibility. Orbit Resources has hit multiple gold, silver and base metal lodes from the first drill holes of a new campaign at its flagship Lewis Ponds project in New South Wales, with key intersections landing outside the boundary of its already substantial 17.52-million-tonne resource. The initial results from the stage two diamond drilling program have delivered on two key fronts, hitting a broad 17-metre intersection grading 1.83 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent within the existing resource, while also defining mineralisation in two previously unmodelled lodes – the Lady Bellmore Lode and the new Hanging-Wall Zone. Orbit Resources’ diamond drilling operations at its Lewis Ponds project near Orange in New South Wales, where fresh results have revealed further gold, silver and base metal mineralisation. The four-hole, 1463-metre campaign at the wholly owned project, 15km east of Orange in the Lachlan Fold Belt, targeted deeper extensions, outlying zones and geophysical anomalies. Lewis Ponds is a volcanic-hosted massive sulphide system, where ancient metal-rich fluids have deposited repeated lenses of precious and base metals. The headlinehole, which landed at the southern end of the Tom’s Lode deposit, returned 17m at 1.83g/t gold equivalent from 347m, including 3m at 3.94g/t from 358m. Another one-metre interval came in at 6.25g/t gold equivalent from 379m, and featured 6.16g/t gold. Gold equivalent combines the estimated recoverable value of multiple metals into a single gold grade. All intervals are downhole, with true widths unconfirmed.

Advertisement

‘These results provide Orbit with a strong pipeline of exploration and technical work at Lewis Ponds as we advance our priority programs into 2027.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit says the Tom’s hit supports continuity within the lower-confidence inferred resource and could help upgrade tonnes to indicated status. Deeper intervals returned 4m at 0.93g/t, 1m at 0.84g/t and 2m at 0.69g/t gold equivalent. Higher in the same hole, Lady Bellmore, a separate lode above Tom’s, returned 6.56m at 1.04g/t from 254.4m. Previously recognised but excluded from the resource, it has now been modelled in three dimensions using historic drilling. The company believes a shallower 3.3m at 0.99g/t from 163.2m hints at a third lode, now dubbed the new Hanging-Wall Zone. About 860m northwest of the Tom’s drill site, a second hole extended another prospect, the Quarry Lode, below previous drilling, returning 5m at 0.92g/t from 121m and 10m at 1.49g/t from 131m. Quarry also lies outside the resource, offering further growth potential. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Stage 2 drilling was designed to strengthen confidence in the existing Lewis Ponds Mineral Resource while testing the potential for mineralisation beyond its current boundaries. Encouragingly, the first two holes have delivered positive results against both objectives.”

Advertisement

Assays from the remaining two holes, which encountered visible sulphides at Tom’s and the established Spicer’s Lode south of Quarry, are due before December ends. Laboratory testing must establish their metal grades. The Quarry hole has been cased ahead of downhole electromagnetic surveying to pinpoint an elusive electrical anomaly that could signal concealed sulphides in the underlying footwall rock and guide further drilling. Lady Bellmore and the new Hanging-Wall Zone also warrant follow-up testing. All results are likely to help Orbit fine-tune its geological model, assess outlying mineralised zones for inclusion in the resource and line up fresh exploration and development targets for 2027. New drill core will also be sent for metallurgical testing, ahead of a potential pre-feasibility study next year. Earlier testwork has already suggested better gravity gold recovery and higher-quality lead concentrate, although those gains are yet to be included in the scoping study. Just 15km east of the regional centre of Orange, Lewis Ponds packs 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver, in addition to zinc, lead and copper. February’s preliminary scoping study flagged a potential 12-year open-pit and underground operation, with a base-case pre-tax net present value of $481 million against $268 million in upfront capital. With NSW stepping up geological exploration across the Lachlan Fold Belt and copper prices remaining elevated, Orbit has reason to look beyond its resource. At Cousin Jack, 350m southeast, June drilling uncovered broad polymetallic sulphides. Immediately southeast, a kilometre-long magnetic target adds intrigue along the broader nine-kilometre mineralised trend.

Advertisement

As drilling continues to uncover fresh mineralisation and extend known lodes, Orbit is steadily building the case for a bigger and potentially more valuable Lewis Ponds resource. And with more assays in the pipeline and a mineralised system that keeps on giving, the company could be closing in on a much larger prize. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? title: How the COP31 agreement fell apart — and what happens next
text:
Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, have come to an end — but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process — or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

No mention of the 'F' word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change — fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels", marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era". But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Türkiye.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Türkiye proposed a compromise — no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy".

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Türkiye and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Türkiye in his speech at the summit opening. While Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship "35 by 35" electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23 per cent at present to 35 per cent by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

The 'COP of action' fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an "implementation COP", focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as "president of negotiations", the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It's possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less — and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were "dead in the water". He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations — including Australia — merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund $450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. "The Pacific did not create this crisis," he declared. "But we will not stand by and wait for others to act."

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

READ MORE The Australians pushing back against a 40 million tonne emissions threat

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which "expressed utmost concern" that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left "nothing on the field" but had faced "unbridgeable red lines".

Hours beforehand, Fijian climate minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was "not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties".

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN secretary-general António Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country — big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.

title: Small businesses spared from online crackdown as crunch time looms for government
text:
In brief Low-risk businesses will be exempt from the government's Digital Duty of Care requirements.

The government still has to reach a deal with the Greens to get the bill through the Senate.

Small businesses will be carved out of the government's plans for online safety crackdowns, as ministers push to get legislation across the line during the final sitting week of the year.

Low-risk business websites will be exempt from Digital Duty of Care requirements if the bill passes, Communications Minister Anika Wells confirmed in a statement.

"The intention of the Digital Duty of Care is to put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur — not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses," she said on Monday.

The onus would be placed back on technology companies to prevent foreseeable harms online.

Labor hopes to reach an agreement with the Greens, who hold the balance of power in the Senate, after the Coalition confirmed it would not support the bill.

The minor party has called for changes that would allow individuals to sue big tech, and for increased crackdown on hate speech associated with race, sexuality, disability and gender.

Greens communications spokesperson Sarah Hanson-Young said she was optimistic a decision could be reached.

"We've seen them (Labor) open the door to allowing for individuals and organisations to take big tech to court," she told the ABC.

"If we can come to an agreement, that is great. If it has to wait until next year, so be it."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has returned from a series of overseas summits to crunch time in parliament, but faces an uphill battle as his popularity has taken a nosedive.

The Labor leader trails his Opposition counterpart, Angus Taylor, as preferred prime minister for the first time, according to a Newspoll published in The Australian on Monday.

Albanese's net approval rating also hit a new low of minus 31, while the Coalition managed to claw back some voter support.

Its primary vote stood at 22 per cent in the latest survey, behind One Nation and Labor, which were tied on 27 per cent.

Labor announced on Monday it would continue to freeze Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme medicines at $25 until the end of 2030.

It comes at a strategic time, as Health Minister Mark Butler tries to get a controversial bill to wind back the health rebate received by Australians over 65 through the Senate.

Separately, Labor will rely on the Opposition to endorse plans for gas companies to set aside up to 20 per cent of their exports for Australian use after a foiled attempt to ram the legislation through the Senate.

The Coalition is not satisfied the bill will ensure future investment or new export opportunities for gas producers after Labor caved on demands to effectively exclude Western Australia from the national scheme.

But there's no hope the Coalition will back a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts — a levy the Greens have said must not exempt funds for tax-exempt organisations such as private schools or religious institutions.

The minor party could also decide whether a 50 per cent capital gains tax discount is reinstated for innovative start-ups.

A last-minute counter-proposal from independent MP Allegra Spender has threatened to send that legislation to a summer inquiry.
