title: 'True icon': Music journalist Molly Meldrum dies aged 83
text:
IN BRIEF Meldrum died early on Monday morning at Richmond's Epworth Hospital.

The legendary music journalist was the beloved face of ABC's Countdown in the 1970s and 80s.

Legendary journalist Ian "Molly" Meldrum has died at the age of 83 after making and breaking music careers for decades.

He died early on Monday morning at Epworth Hospital in Richmond, Melbourne, after a long illness, his family said in a statement.

"He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him," they said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also paid tribute to Meldrum.

"With an interview style that was inimitable and an enthusiasm that was uncontainable, Molly Meldrum loved music almost as much as we loved him," Albanese said in a social media post.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"On Countdown and beyond, he championed Australian artists and brought international acts to our shores. He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace.

"And over the years, as he implored us to do ourselves a favour, he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him."

His longtime friend and manager, Mark Klemens of Profile Talent Management, said Australia had lost a "true icon".

"A man who opened doors for so many and entertained millions of people here and around the world," Klemens said on Monday.

Meldrum faced a serious health battle after falling from a ladder in 2011 and has had several health issues since. Source: AAP / James Ross

"He was unconventional and wonderfully unpredictable, but always caring, always funny and always down to earth, with a passion the rest of us could only envy.

"He made the most of his life, and boy, was it a full one. Rest in peace, Molly."

Who was Molly Meldrum?

Born in the regional Victorian town of Orbost in 1943, Meldrum forged a career in the music industry, becoming the face of ABC's wildly popular Countdown program in the 1970s and 80s.

He was introduced to the music business while working as a roadie for his friend's band, The Groop, and through a weekly column he wrote for the pop music newspaper Go-Set.

His unique, "camp" writing style earned him the nickname Molly from a DJ friend.

He moved to London in the late 1960s, where he met his idols John Lennon and Paul McCartney.

After returning to Australia, Meldrum's major break came in 1974 when he was commissioned to create a music show for the ABC.

Countdown was a phenomenal success and catapulted Meldrum into the spotlight.

Meldrum was a devoted supporter of the St Kilda Football Club. Source: AAP / Rob Prezioso

He became synonymous with the Australian music industry and Countdown acted as a springboard for local bands Skyhooks and Sherbet and international artists including ABBA and Cyndi Lauper.

His laid-back interview style made him the go-to guy for many artists like Elton John and Rod Stewart.

From Bruce Springsteen and Beyonce to Madonna and Michael Jackson, few have had a bad word to say about Meldrum.

"Molly is often the only person in the world who gets the interview," according to Australian music promoter Michael Chugg, who was a close friend of Meldrum's for more than 40 years.

"That's the regard he is held in."

But there was one interview that Meldrum himself admitted didn't go well.

In 1977 he nervously interviewed Prince Charles and was famously reprimanded by the visiting royal for referring to the Queen as "your mum".

While co-hosting Countdown with Dolly Parton, he was starstruck.

"I've never been more nervous doing a show in my life," he told the country music superstar in 1979.

Countdown was cancelled in 1987, but Meldrum had become bigger than the show itself.

Besides fronting Countdown, Meldrum was also known for his success as a music producer.

He worked with Australian star Russell Morris to produce his classic song The Real Thing, while also producing hits for Ronnie Burns, Colleen Hewett, Supernaut and The Ferrets.

In 1985 he hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid, Oz for Africa.

A year later he was made a Member of the Order of Australia for services to the fostering of international relief and to youth.

He added an ARIA Special Achievement Award for services to the industry to the collection in 1993.

Other TV appearances included a regular segment on long-running variety show Hey Hey It's Saturday called Molly's Melodrama.

In 2004, he joined Christine Anu and John Paul Young as a judge on Popstars Live, and was also a producer on the series.

Ian 'Molly' Meldrum at his 80th birthday celebration alongside his beloved dog. Source: Getty / Sam Tabone/WireImage

Meldrum faced a serious health battle in December 2011 after falling from a ladder while hanging Christmas decorations. He was placed in an induced coma due to severe head lacerations.

In 2014, he was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame and released his autobiography, which he wrote with music journalist Jeff Jenkins.

He was a long-time supporter of the St Kilda AFL team and Melbourne Storm NRL side.

He also loved his string of loyal dogs, who were all named Ziggy.

Meldrum is survived by his brothers, Brian and Robert, and by Morgan, whom he helped raise and regarded as his son, along with Morgan's wife, Crystal, and their son, Jason, who Meldrum cherished as a grandson.

His long-time partner Yan Wongngam cared for Meldrum with great love and devotion, especially through his final years.

Meldrum's family have requested privacy as they grieve.

title: Liberals, Greens label Labor 'worse than disappointing' over role in COP31 breakdown
text:
In brief A final agreement was dramatically rejected at COP31 on Sunday after the conference ran two days over schedule.

Türkiye and Australia had tried to rally support behind a global goal to electrify the world economy.

The Opposition leader has called on Labor's Chris Bowen to resign after the COP31 climate talks ended without agreement, while the Greens have criticised what they called "a comprehensive failure of leadership from Labor".

Bowen, the climate change and energy minister who served as COP31 negotiations chair under a co-hosting deal struck with Türkiye, unsuccessfully sought to broker consensus among nearly 200 nations.

However, he ultimately conceded he could not overcome what he called "unbridgeable red lines", partly related to the inclusion or omission of references to fossil fuels in the agreement, which was dramatically rejected on Sunday.

It was a chaotic finale to a United Nations climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world.

Bowen's Liberal energy counterpart, Dan Tehan, said if Bowen doesn't resign, the prime minister should sack him.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Chris Bowen should resign today," Tehan said in a statement.

"Australian taxpayers have funded Chris Bowen’s $150m COP pretensions, only for the so-called president to embarrass Australia on the world stage by making jokes about his penis. Of course, the one thing Chris Bowen has not failed to do is spend taxpayers’ money."

Tehan was referring to a gaffe by Bowen and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who were recorded joking about phone radiation and penises while waiting for a meeting to begin at the conference. Albanese later apologised for the hot-mic incident.

From the start, the Coalition has been critical of Australia's bid to host the summit and has lashed the costs of co-hosting the talks.

Liberal leader Angus Taylor later echoed the call for Bowen to resign, saying "he's not up to the job".

"We should scrap net zero, that what should happen tomorrow and we should unleash the natural resources we have in this country, our oil, our coal, our gas, our uranium."

Meanwhile, Greens leader David Shoebridge said the government was "doing what it can to destroy the global action we need for a safe climate."

"At the end of COP 31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific neighbours.

"This is worse than disappointing."

Australian climate groups have also expressed disappointment at the lack of agreement, with some putting the blame on Bowen and Albanese.

"As president of negotiations, Australia failed to broker an agreement when wealthy nations blocked progress on climate finance," Denise Cauchi, CEO of Climate Action Network Australia, said.

"Instead of implementing the transition away from fossil fuels agreed to three years ago and the just transition agreed last year, Australia and Türkiye caved to 700 carbon capture lobbyists and almost gifted industry the biggest loophole for coal, oil and gas expansion in the history of COP."

Former Greens leader and CEO of Australian Conservation Foundation Adam Bandt was also scathing.

"Countries understandably rejected an Australia-led deal that failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them," Bandt said.

"The prime minister's snub of the UN secretary-general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit. The UN secretary-general urged Australia and Türkiye to make this the COP that staves off climate collapse by reining in coal and gas, but the prime minister refused to listen."

UN secretary-general António Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at COP31, expressed deep dismay as the talks broke down.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," the outgoing UN chief said in a statement.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision ... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," Bowen, told reporters.

More than 49 hours after the summit was supposed to end, COP31 president and Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum banged the gavel to conclude the marathon talks.

'Fraught geopolitical environment'

Bowen said the summit backdrop was "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory" as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity.

Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching "cover decision" to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis.

But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas.

The negotiations stalled as oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal.

"We will not endorse a cover decision ... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

"And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

Panama, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected and, as the deal imploded, COP31 became the longest climate summit on record.

'World cannot afford a repeat'

The outcome revived memories of the failed Copenhagen summit of 2009 and raised fresh doubts about the effectiveness of climate diplomacy.

"It certainly fell short today," said UN climate chief Simon Stiell, describing progress over the marathon fortnight of negotiations in Antalya as "limited".

"The world cannot afford a repeat."

Frustrated by the inertia, countries are pushing ahead outside the COP process.

READ MORE The controversial export title Australia is on track to earn

Around 60 countries joined a first-of-its-kind conference in April on phasing out fossil fuels while several nations at COP31 unveiled their own plans to exit coal, oil and gas.

In a last-ditch bid for compromise, COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia could only muster a veiled reference to fossil fuels in the final text.

But the pact also took fire for retaining a call to expand carbon capture — a costly technology championed by the fossil fuel industry.

title: More Australians are avoiding the doctor. What's the real cost?
text:
IN BRIEF Half of Australians are opting to forgo health care to save money, according to new research.

Almost 20 per cent of those surveyed by researchers were not satisfied with previous healthcare services.

Half of Australians are putting up with pain rather than see a doctor or dentist because of the cost.

A survey of more than 5,000 people found almost half decided to forgo certain healthcare interventions over the last 12 months.

Lack of affordability was the most common reason why people delayed or went without care, according to the Consumers Health Forum of Australia's national consumer sentiment survey, released on Monday.

More than two-thirds of that group put off seeing a dentist, close to half did not fill a prescription and a third did not see a doctor, the 80-page report found.

Consumers Health Forum of Australia chief executive Elizabeth Deveny said the findings described a health system splitting in two.

"We have a health system where there are the haves and the have-nots. The gap between them is where people are getting hurt," she said.

"Healthcare decisions are made at the kitchen table and weighed against rent, groceries and everything else due that week. For a lot of people, choices are becoming impossible."

Dental care in particular was identified as the most expensive health service, with nine in 10 respondents agreeing that it should be considered part of Medicare and partially subsidised.

Close to six in 10 had delayed or avoided dental care and reported pain, difficulty eating and even losing teeth.

Brisbane resident Gaylene Smith, 74, has been supporting her sister in Darwin who was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018.

She praised the medical team surrounding her but worried that patients were "fading away" under the strain of rising costs and being unable to keep up with medical bills.

Her sister needed medication to treat psoriasis, which developed as a side effect of the cancer therapy and cost about $4,000 per month before recently being listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

"It would have been nice for there to have been a process [so] that she could have accessed that either cheaply or cheaper than $4,000 a month," Smith told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

The survey findings also suggested that healthcare experiences were shaped not only by financial resources and health needs, but also by whether services were accessible and culturally appropriate.

Despite the access and equity challenges, 81 per cent of respondents who had received health care said they were satisfied with their care.

title: The data centre lobby's growing influence: 100 meetings, millions in political payments
text:
IN BRIEF A new report has found 11 data centre companies and their lobbying firms spent $3.4 million in the past four years.

It says the payments went predominantly to the Labor Party and the Australian Business Council.

Data centre companies have held more than 100 meetings with state premiers and ministers in the past three years, and given $3.4 million to parties and industry bodies.

That's according to Transparency International, which has partially captured the industry's lobbying efforts and people-to-people links as the sector's footprint expands across Australia to at least 283 planned or operational data centres.

The information is only partially captured because Western Australia, South Australia, the Northern Territory and the federal government do not give access to ministerial diaries, meaning the engagement might be the tip of the iceberg.

Queensland's David Crisafulli has held 13 meetings with data centre executives since 2023, the most of any premier captured by the figures.

They included three meetings with ADC in May 2026 and three meetings with NextDC in three weeks from August 2026, just before Queensland announced a fast-track data centre approval process.

Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the level of access to decision-makers might concern Australians, given polling shows deep divides on the merits of such centres.

"They have huge amounts of resources, access to ministers, access to third-party lobbyists and that gives them a huge advantage, particularly when local community groups are being shut out from decision-making processes," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.

"This erodes trust in our democracy and risks decisions favouring private not public interests."

The report tallies payments of $3.4 million from 11 data centre companies and their lobbying firms in the past four years, predominantly to the Labor Party and Australian Business Council.

Several data centre firms gave six-figure amounts, including Microsoft ($414,700), Macquarie Technology ($346,900), Goodman ($308,000) and Amazon ($254,346), while Anacta, a lobbying firm for Anthropic, gave $468,107.

READ MORE Stocks tumble as AI bubble fears prompt market sell-off, with Anthropic shares falling

A large chunk of the funding was not categorised as a donation but declared in other ways, suggesting membership of a party's business forum or seats at events involving senior party members.

Moore said these donations created a perception of "pay to play".

The watchdog organisation believes lawmakers risk "policy capture" by the industry and wants improved disclosure of lobbying, staff movements between government and industry and funding.

Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan will launch a reform push for just that on Monday, although her legislation will fail without government support.

Ryan's national lobbying bill would replace the existing code of conduct with a legislated scheme, including beefed-up reporting requirements that also capture in-house lobbyists.

"We need to know who ministers meet with, where, when and why because that will go a long way toward restoring trust in evidence-based decision-making," she told AAP.

Federal ministers currently dodge requests to provide their diaries under freedom of information processes.

The bill also enforces a stand-down period for ministers, political staffers and high-ranking public servants taking lobbying jobs after public office.

Transparency International details examples of the "revolving door" between government and industry, including a new hire for OpenAI plucked from the office of AI in the prime minister's department.

"People lose faith in government decision-making when they see people go straight from the positions where those decisions are made into the industries that commercially benefit," Ryan said.

She hoped to meet with Attorney-General Michelle Rowland in the coming week to garner support.

title: Australia's first GLP-1 weight-loss tablets are here. How do they compare to injections?
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's first GLP-1s in tablet form have hit the market.

The two types available have differing pros and cons.

The arrival of GLP-1 tablets is giving Australians more choice in weight-loss treatment, with experts saying the new medications have broadly similar effects to existing injections.

The Wegovy tablet, made by Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, became the first of its kind to be cleared by Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) this month and landed on pharmacy shelves on Friday.

Until now, GLP-1 medications approved for weight management in Australia have been administered through weekly injections.

A second weight-loss pill, Foundayo, made by US pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, has also received TGA approval.

Both medications work by mimicking the action of GLP-1, a hormone released by the gut after eating that helps regulate blood sugar levels and appetite.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Use of Wegovy, Ozempic and other GLP-1 drugs for diabetes has surged in recent years. In Australia, sales of these medications increased almost tenfold between May 2020 and April 2025, according to research from the University of New South Wales, with at least half a million people estimated to be regularly using them.

While these drugs were traditionally used for diabetes, some have since been approved for weight management.

Teacher and mother-of-six Kim Roberts has been giving herself weekly weight-loss drug injections for the past three years after a heart attack led to the discovery of a genetic cholesterol condition.

She plans to switch to taking Wegovy as a daily tablet.

"It will just fit in with what I do on a day-to-day basis," she told the Australian Associated Press.

The 46-year-old said the drug has helped her to lose around 30kg, learn to eat better and manage her condition.

Mother-of-six and teacher Kim Roberts is looking forward to the weight loss drug in pill format. Source: AAP / Supplied/PR Image

How does it compare to injections?

Professor Priya Sumithran, head of the obesity and metabolic medicine group at Monash University, said the new tablets could appeal to people who have been reluctant to use injectable medications.

While the pills offer a new way to take the drug, she said there are few significant differences in the way they work and the associated side effects.

"I think the considerations would mostly be up to personal preference — whether you prefer to take a once-a-week injection, [or] whether you prefer to take a once-a-day tablet," she said.

Drugs such as Wegovy and Ozempic have been available in Australia as injectables only. Source: AAP / Jason Bergman/Sipa USA

The tablets also have similar side effects to injectable GLP-1 medications, with nausea, vomiting and indigestion among the most common.

Louise Baur, an expert in child and adolescent obesity at the University of Sydney, said a daily medication can bring its own challenges and lifestyle adjustments for some.

"You have to take [the Wegovy pill] at least half an hour before eating, and so that means a routine that you have to get into," she said.

Unlike Wegovy, Foundayo can be taken at any time of day without the same restrictions.

Experts have cautioned against viewing GLP-1 medications as a quick fix for weight loss, but rather as part of a broader approach to managing obesity that includes health eating, physical activity and ongoing medical support.

How much do they cost?

The price of Wegovy tablets varies by dose, costing between $260 and $395 a month.

It's not listed on Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, though it was recommended by an advisory committee nearly a year ago.

The federal government is in negotiations with Wegovy's manufacturer to bring it onto the scheme for a small cohort of patients.

It would bring the price down to $25 per script or $7.70 for concession card holders.

Source: SBS News

Terri-Lynne South, a GP with a special interest in obesity management at the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, said affordability remains a barrier for patients.

"Like the injectable, it's only available on private prescription. Until obesity medicines are subsidised, access will be determined by what people can afford rather than by clinical need," she said.

"Obesity is a chronic disease, and weight regain is common when treatment stops, so it is important to discuss the long-term plan with patients, including cost, before starting."

What's next for weight-loss medications?

Sumithran said nearly 30 medications are undergoing late-stage clinical trials, with some combining GLP-1 with other hormones to potentially improve their effectiveness or target particular health conditions.

She said the expanding range of treatments could eventually allow doctors to better tailor medications to individual patients.

"I think the interesting thing about those additional hormones is what specific benefits we will get from those," she said.

Researchers are also investigating the use of existing medications in children and adolescents.

Baur said two recent studies had examined the use of GLP-1 medications in children and adolescents, including the first trial of injectable semaglutide in children aged six to 12.

However, she said, the development of new medications needs to be accompanied by greater efforts to improve access to affordable treatment and support and tackle the underlying drivers of obesity.

She called for a future in which people living with obesity could access effective treatment without experiencing stigma, including within the healthcare system.

title: 'Reject any implications': Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain
text:
In brief Cricket Australia says it backs Pat Cummins as captain.

The organisation's board voted unanimously to keep him in the position.

Pat Cummins will remain Australia's Test cricket captain despite controversy over his role in the sandpaper scandal.

Cummins' tenure as skipper had been questioned amid conflicting accounts of what he knew about Australia's ball tampering in the 2018 South African series.

Following a board meeting, Cricket Australia (CA) on Saturday confirmed Cummins would stay as captain for the three-Test series against New Zealand starting 9 December in Perth, issuing a statement rejecting any implication that his "integrity has been compromised".

"In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA Board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian cricket and the welfare of all concerned," CA wrote in a statement.

"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."

The statement revealed that CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met with Cummins in Sydney on Friday.

That followed the announcement that players from the 2018 series would be invited to participate in an independent forum, that would allow them to give their accounts of the incident.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa," Boon said.

"We have learned from that experience, and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins said he backed the forum and intended to participate.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there," the fast bowler said.

"All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins, who has held the captaincy since late November 2021, has steadfastly denied any knowledge of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball in the 2018 series in South Africa.

His stance has been repudiated by Cameron Bancroft, Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers; all teammates of the paceman on the infamous tour eight years ago.

Cummins has described Khawaja's claims the entire touring party knew of scheming to tamper with the ball in South Africa as "nonsense" and has been backed Josh Hazlewood.

Hazelwood said he would have considered quitting if Cummins was made to stand down.

"I think I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," Hazlewood told NewsCorp.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile on the last few days from different people. I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Meanwhile, Steve Smith will be back in the spotlight after being included in the NSW side for the final round of Sheffield Shield games before Australia name a squad for the New Zealand series.

The star batsman was stripped of the Test captaincy and received a 12-month ban from all international and Australian domestic cricket for his role in the cheating saga, but the 37-year-old has maintained his silence amid the fresh furore.

Smith hasn't played any cricket since suffering a neck injury in the second Test on last month's tour of South Africa, but was named in the Blues' squad for the SCG match against Queensland, starting Sunday.

He trained on Friday, but arrived through a back entrance and media were locked out of watching him bat in the nets.

Spinner Nathan Lyon, who was also part of the 2018 contingent was also included in the 12-man line-up, while other members of the national cohort Cummins, Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were left out.

title: The traps, dodgy deals and scams to watch for this Black Friday and Cyber Monday
text:
In brief Many retailers have kicked off sales ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Consumer groups say it's important for shoppers to watch for a range of misleading sales tactics.

One of the biggest retail sales periods of the year is underway. But with it comes the risk of scams, misleading marketing and deals that aren't really deals.

The Australian consumer watchdog says it is monitoring websites, emails and social media for misleading sales advertising.

"Consumers continue to look for the best prices and may delay major purchases until Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of good value and legitimate discounts," Catriona Lowe, deputy chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), said earlier this month.

"Consumers should be able to trust that the advertised savings and discount prices are genuine, but we know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not."

Black Friday and Cyber Monday fall on 27 and 30 November this year, but many retailers have already kicked off their sales.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The ACCC said it is cracking down on misleading sales tactics, including "sitewide" discounts that exclude many products, limited-time offers that continue past their advertised end date, and false claims that stock is running low.

It is also scrutinising discounts advertised against prices that products were never — or have not recently been — sold at.

Here are some of the tactics bargain hunters should watch for.

Deadlines and timers

Setting deadlines is an "age-old trick" designed to rush shoppers into a purchase, according to financial comparison site Canstar.

During Black Friday and Cyber Monday, many sites use countdown timers showing how long shoppers have left to secure a deal.

Businesses are permitted to use these timers, but only if the deadline is genuine.

A number of major retailers were fined following the ACCC's sweep of last year's Black Friday sales advertising.

The ACCC alleged two of the businesses advertised that their sales would end at a certain time, but the discounts continued beyond that deadline.

One retailer offered an even bigger discount in a new sale after the earlier countdown ended, the watchdog said.

Scarcity warnings

Countdowns aren't the only way retailers create a sense of urgency.

Canstar also points to low-stock alerts such as "Hurry! Only two left in your size", virtual waiting rooms to access sales and messages suggesting multiple people are viewing an item.

These messages can make shoppers feel as though they need to act quickly or miss out.

Watch out for fine print

Stores will sometimes advertise deals of "up to 50 per cent off", but only discount a few items to that extent.

The detail clarifying that could be buried in a fine-print disclaimer.

The ACCC says retailers must ensure their sales and discount claims are clear and accurate, and that fine-print qualifications do not conflict with the overall message of the advertisement.

"Retailers should not be relying on fine print disclaimers or exclusions to qualify the headline message of a promotion," Lowe said.

Exaggerated savings

The watchdog will also be cracking down on ads that show misleading markdowns.

For example, if a retailer advertises that the price of a washing machine has been slashed from $500 down to $300, it suggests shoppers are saving $200.

But if the washing machine was recently priced at $400, the real saving compared with that price is only $100.

"Consumers are encouraged to focus on the end price of a product, not on promotional claims," the ACCC said.

"This includes checking for any exclusions or conditions, and comparing prices between retailers and over time where possible. They should carefully consider the advertised price and buy only if the price and time is right for them."

Scams

Buying and selling scams accounted for nearly 59 per cent of Scamwatch reports involving a financial loss in the first nine months of 2026.

These scams involve fraudsters posing as buyers or sellers to steal money, including through fake shopping websites and fraudulent profiles on legitimate platforms.

The government agency says scammers can look like businesses that you know and trust. Shoppers should be wary of social media stores selling products at very low prices, unfamiliar websites, and links received via email.

"Always check the web address, and if you don’t know the store, read reviews, or better yet, walk away," Canstar suggests.

title: Stocks tumble as AI bubble fears prompt market sell-off, with Anthropic shares falling
text:
In brief An AI bust in 2027 is a growing worry for investors.

AI firm Anthropic's share price has fallen after a bumper market debut.

Tech shares nosedived in the United States on Friday, local time, (Saturday AEDT) and dragged stocks into the red around the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations.

Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of US$83 ($123) to over US$110 ($166) on Thursday despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below US$89 ($134) at the close on Friday.

"The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said.

While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled on Friday, closing down more than five per cent.

New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 3.7 per cent on Friday, extending a run of losses.

"The disappointing performance has reinforced concerns about elevated AI valuations and the enormous capital commitments required to support the industry's growth," said Briefing.com analysts in a note.

"Neither Anthropic's IPO nor Nvidia's strong earnings has been sufficient to restore confidence, with investors continuing to sell into rebound attempts.

James Reilly of Capital Economics said the fall in tech stocks could "have further to run".

He labelled the prospect of an "AI bust in 2027" his central forecast and a growing worry for investors.

"This doesn't mean we think the technology is a dud, nor that demand will collapse. But the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding," he wrote.

Traders have also been spooked by the US commerce department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector.

It comes after Nvidia's high-profile founder and CEO Jensen Huang had to resign following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

The chip giant, which has endured a long period of losses, slumped by 14.01 per cent at the close in New York on Friday, despite posting massive profits earlier in the week.

In Asian trading Friday, the Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei stock markets — home to the region's leading AI-linked firms — tumbled between five and 6.2 per cent.

Europe's main stock markets all fell back significantly by close of trading, with shares in French video game maker Ubisoft slumping more than 20 per cent after it posted a bigger first-half loss than expected.

The report came amid the worldwide hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto 6, the latest in the hugely popular Rockstar Games series, which took a record US$3.79 billion ($5.72 billion) in opening day retail sales this week.

title: Trump's administration is sending mixed signals on chips, China and AI
text:
In brief The US is seeking to combat the spread of Chinese open-weight AI models and restrict access to high-end chips from US companies.

The Chinese embassy in Washington says China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "serve no one's interests".

The United States approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips to Chinese companies over six months, as the Trump administration reportedly considers requiring US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.

The US House of Representatives' foreign affairs committee said on Friday that between December 2025 and May 2026, the US government approved 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD.

All four companies are on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies. The chips sold included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X chips.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the committee's documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips.

Former US president Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

Trump gave the green light in December for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to approved companies in China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.

The US commerce department said its approach to H200 licensing "is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial".

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes". The California-based company added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China".

Meanwhile, AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations".

Earlier this week, the US said it would further restrict China's access to high-end chips from US companies, citing national security concerns and saying it would close "dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years".

The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

The announcement came shortly after longtime Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company following reports he had an affair with a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres. The company has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

US intelligence officials have alleged the woman was a Chinese spy, an accusation China has denied.

Before resigning as Nvidia CEO, Huang had lobbied the Trump administration to allow more of his company's chip sales to China, warning that the controls would otherwise boost the Chinese chip industry's competitiveness.

On Friday, California announced it was investigating whether Nvidia misled the public and investors about its chips ending up in China, despite federal export controls.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," US attorney-general Rob Bonta said in a statement.

'Name and shame' campaign

At the same time, the US is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or China, according to Reuters.

The US treasury department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb.

The short-term rental platform uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent.

Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites.

It's unclear whether the idea is gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process.

But its consideration underscores an emerging push by the US to combat the spread of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Open-weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt.

The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI.

Neither the White House, the US treasury department, nor Alibaba have commented on the proposal.

Airbnb said in a statement to Reuters that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected".

The Chinese embassy in Washington said China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests".

"We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests," it said.

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

But some within the US, including officials in Trump's administration, fear China is using such models — like Kimi, DeepSeek, or Qwen — to hook US companies into becoming dependent on Chinese AI.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft through distillation of US models.

Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones to lower the cost of training a powerful new AI tool.

Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by OTSP director Michael Kratsios, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a push by the US state department to highlight such behaviour to foreign counterparts.

title: A decade on from Brexit, EU and UK relations reach a 'turning point'
text:
In brief The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, 10 years after the UK voted to leave the bloc.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and isolated.

The United Kingdom and the European Union have agreed to remove barriers to trade and expand travel opportunities for young people as they pledged to rebuild their strained ties with an "ambitious and dynamic" relationship.

But they left big decisions about softening or reversing Brexit for another day.

In a joint statement on Friday night AEDT after a summit in Brussels, the UK and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap border checks on plant and animal products, cut carbon taxes on some exports by linking their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other's countries for up to three years.

Other areas remain a work in progress, with the two sides giving themselves six months to reach an agreement on the level of university fees for EU students in the UK and vice versa.

The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, a decade after the UK voted to leave the EU and six years after the divorce became final.

Supporters of Brexit argued that leaving the EU's vast free-trade area and web of rules would let the UK take back control of its borders, laws and economy, and strike new trade deals around the world.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and more isolated, and new deals with countries including Australia and Japan have not made up for the economic hit from erecting barriers between the UK and its closest and biggest economic partners.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the deal is "a turning point" in EU-UK relations, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a "historic moment".

"This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe," he said.

This was only the second EU-UK summit since the UK became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from electricity markets to manufacturing rules.

Burnham said the summit was a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.

He said the two sides are "rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago" and "building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market".

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc.

READ MORE UK prime minister says Russia meddled in Brexit vote, pushes for EU return

But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of UK voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

"We remain open to have the closest possible relationship," European Council president António Costa said.

But he also recalled the obligations of EU membership, including single-market principles on the free movement of goods, services, people and capital.

Burnham says closer ties will ease the cost of living

Burnham pitched the package of agreements as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people." He said the deals could bring in £17 billion ($33 billion) a year and add 0.5 per cent to the UK's economic output.

British retailers welcomed the deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products, which will make it cheaper and easier for UK businesses to export to Europe.

"Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow," said Alex Freudmann, managing director of food at Marks and Spencer.

Freudmann said the announcement "is a major step forward".

But nothing in UK-EU relations is ever quick or simple. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in the UK rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the UK has resisted.

An EU official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue. The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.

Talks are also continuing on the UK's desire to be included in the bloc’s "made in Europe" rules, which favor European manufacturers for public projects over rivals from China or elsewhere.

Critics say the deals are a betrayal of Brexit

To get the deals, the UK must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines the UK's independence.

Nigel Farage, leader of the euroskeptic, anti-immigration party Reform UK, told reporters in Brussels that Burnham had taken "the first step, incrementally, to take us back into membership of the European Union".

The war in Ukraine, and the UK's military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and the summit produced pledges of stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the UK rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven UK prime ministers over the last decade and want clarity about the country’s intentions.

Von der Leyen said that a lot has changed in their relations since the Brexit vote, including the pandemic and Russia’s war on Ukraine. She said that the EU is "totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture, the bigger picture" of what ties could look like in the future.

Burnham said he wanted the two sides to do that brainstorming before their next summit, probably a year from now.

For now, Burnham remains bound by the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or friction-less single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the UK

He acknowledged the agreements are "the limit of what we can achieve" before a national election.

title: The controversial export title Australia is on track to earn
text:
In Brief A new report from the International Energy Agency shows Australia set to become the world's biggest coal exporter.

The organisation said uptake in renewables will continue to grow in coming decades.

Australia could become the world's largest exporter of coal within the next decade, according to analysis from an international energy body.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has published its annual World Energy Outlook since 1999, offering multiple views of potential energy futures based on that year's developments.

In this year's report, the agency provided a cautious view based on current policies, another based on policies announced but not yet enacted and a third more ambitious view seeking to reduce emissions alongside alternatives for potential impacts of the conflict in the Middle East.

Since the organisation was established in 1974, energy demand has nearly tripled worldwide. Coal has been the fastest-growing fossil fuel since 2020, with Indonesia and Australia among the top exporters.

By 2035, this would make Australia the largest supplier of coal, with the margin growing further by 2050.

The report described the disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as the "largest threat to energy security in history".

"The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system," Fatih Birol, IEA executive director, said.

"I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before."

The report said consumers were frequently facing higher prices, as countries' fuel stockpiles depleted.

The IEA suggested renewable energy could rise from 33 per cent of global electricity generation to 50 per cent by 2035 and 66 per cent by 2050. Alongside the growth in renewable energy production, the oil and gas supply shock has accelerated solar, battery and electric vehicle adoption in several countries.

Solar has the largest projected growth, then onshore and offshore wind, hydropower, bioenergy and geothermal.

The IEA said the longer uncertainty persists over the Middle East conflict, the more likely countries will seek to diversify their energy supply and adopt policy to better enable it.

"Countries will pursue different pathways, reflecting their resources, circumstances and priorities," Birol said.

"But all have a stake in building a more secure, affordable and sustainable energy system — and in effective cooperation to achieve that goal."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese joined Kylie Minogue, Jimmy Barnes and Blondie in paying tribute to Australian music legend Ian “Molly” Meldrum following his death at the age of 83. As the host of Countdown, Meldrum brought local and international music to our television screens in a must-watch program the likes of which this country had never seen. With an often bumbling, loose interviewing style, he won the hearts of viewers and artists alike. Molly Meldrum has died aged 83. He had long been ill and died at 5.30am on Monday at the Epworth Hospital in Richmond, in inner Melbourne. He will be granted a state funeral. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Australian music legend, journalist, producer and cultural icon Ian Alexander ‘Molly’ Meldrum AM … He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him,” his family said via a statement.

“Affectionately dubbed ‘The Guru’, Meldrum was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music. He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them … He lived and breathed music, believing in its power to unite, to inspire and to lift up young musicians.” In 1974, Meldrum helped develop Countdown, working as a talent co-ordinator, interviewer and presenter on the show. His catchphrase “Do yourself a favour” entered the Australian vernacular. Loading On the show, he championed acts like AC/DC and Russell Morris and brought international icons including Elton John, ABBA and Madonna to Australian audiences. After Countdown ended, Meldrum joined Hey Hey It’s Saturday, hosting the music and entertainment segment Molly’s Melodrama. He also hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid (Oz for Africa ) in 1985.

Gavin Wood, who worked with Meldrum on Countdown, described his friend and former colleague as “one of the craziest, most colourful, funniest and most beautiful people you could ever have the pleasure of meeting”. ‘There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him.’ Gavin Wood “He was absolutely one of a kind, and it was a privilege to know him,” Wood wrote on Facebook. “What he has done for the Australian music industry is simply phenomenal. His contribution, passion, enthusiasm and unwavering commitment to Australian artists helped shape an entire generation of music and entertainment. “There will never be another Molly Meldrum. Kylie Minogue posted that she would turn up the music in his honour. “As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room and dreaming of how music might become part of my life,” she wrote. Floral tributes were placed outside Meldrum’s home in the Melbourne suburb of Richmond on Monday following news of his death. Simon Schluter Jimmy Barnes said on Instagram that the impact of appearing on Countdown was immediate. “Our shows went from pubs to bigger pubs to big halls in a matter of months. Molly exposed us to a huge music audience we could never have reached and we were always thankful to him for that.” In a tribute posted to X, the prime minister said Meldrum “loved music almost as much as we loved him”.

“He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace. And over the years ... he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him,” Albanese wrote. He was an advocate of Australian music, talent scout, journalist, producer and broadcaster who helped shape the soundtrack of our nation,” he said. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said Meldrum’s family had asked for a state funeral and that he would honour that wish. Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson paid her respects in a statement, saying that “Australia has lost a legend, and Victoria has lost one of its favourite sons”. text:

PoliticsFederalFederal budget ‘No use pretending otherwise’: Chalmers warns of tough year ahead as jobless and inflation forecasts worsen Shane Wright Updated November 23, 2026 — 5:32pm ,first published 3:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has pledged to produce “budget-sized” spending cuts to put downward pressure on inflation after revealing a bleak economic outlook far worse than expected, with unemployment on track to breach 5 per cent. As economists rate the chances of a local recession at up to fifty-fifty, Chalmers used an address to parliament to warn that the country faced “difficult times full of serious risks”, with economic growth to slip below 2 per cent for the next two years. Jim Chalmers is preparing Australians for a tough economic year ahead. Renee Nowytarger Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese have been under fire over the state of both the economy and the budget, with inflation at 4.3 per cent, unemployment at a five-year-high and real wages falling – all while the budget is in deficit. The Reserve Bank has pushed official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, although financial markets now believe it will have to start cutting by September to help prop up the economy.

Advertisement

Chalmers conceded the economy faced strong headwinds that households were already starting to feel. He said higher oil prices meant inflation was now likely to remain in the mid-threes until near the end of next year. Interest rates would also weigh on household spending. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “This means GDP growth could slow from 2.3 per cent last year to well below 2 per cent for the next two years. Treasury expects unemployment to stay below pre-pandemic averages but now peak higher, above 5 per cent,” he said. “2026 has been a very tough year for our people, our economy and the world. No use pretending otherwise. Interest rates are biting, unemployment is rising, prices are going up, wages aren’t keeping pace and families are hurting.” All forecasts are worse than what Chalmers announced in his May budget. At the time, he forecast economic growth would slow to 1.75 per cent this year before recovering to 2.25 per cent in 2027-28, that inflation would average 2.5 per cent, and that the jobless rate would remain around 4.5 per cent.

Advertisement

Economists with NAB on Monday said the outlook for the jobs market could be even worse, forecasting unemployment to reach 5.5 per cent early in 2028. At that level, the jobless rate would be at its highest level – outside of the pandemic – since 2018. In May, Chalmers forecast the budget would show a deficit of $31.5 billion this financial year, followed by shortfalls of $31 billion, $34.4 billion and $25.3 billion in the three following years. Tax as a share of the economy was forecast to reach 23.8 per cent, its highest point since the 2005-06 record of 24.2 per cent. Government spending as a share of the economy was expected to reach 26.8 per cent. Chalmers said in the short-term the budget deficit was likely to be a little smaller this year but deficits would likely be larger from 2027-28 onwards. The economy is already a little smaller than anticipated, which meant tax and spending as a share of GDP were likely to be slightly higher, even with savings in the mid-year update.

Advertisement

The treasurer said those savings would be spread across the budget, although he argued the government would not slash expenditure. Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market “At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on. We understand and embrace our role in the fight against inflation. Our decisions will deliver a modest net saving despite all these pressures,” he said. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused Chalmers of overseeing a deliberate policy of inflation and policy shock that was undermining confidence among businesses and households. “The prime minister and the treasurer have become the Thelma and Louise of the Australian economy, driving small business and jobs and opportunity off a cliff,” he said.

Advertisement

That cliff could be a domestic recession. HSBC Australia chief economist Paul Bloxham said the deterioration in the economy, particularly in the housing market, meant the chances of the economy going backwards were little better than a coin flip. “We forecast that growth will stall in the coming quarters and see a fifty-fifty chance of a recession,” he said. Bloxham said the AI boom and its call on global savings, on top of the war against Iran, meant interest rates around the world were likely to remain persistently higher than they were before the pandemic. Those higher interest rates are already hitting the budget. Chalmers revealed that if interest on Australian government bonds had remained at 5.4 per cent, a level they reached in early October, then the nation’s interest bill would be $40 billion higher over the next decade.

Advertisement

Loading Bloxham said the government’s changes to housing taxes meant first home buyers were likely to enter a more affordable property market next year. “First home buyers are likely to return to the market more fervently when there are signs the housing price downswing is bottoming, but with fewer investors the eventual upswing is likely to be more subdued than in the past,” he said. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said while the chances of a recession were high, the strength of the AI construction boom and the global economy, plus a recent dip in the Australian dollar, would help support local activity. “However, we would put the risk of recession at a high, and still rising at 40 per cent,” he said.

Advertisement

“The rising trend in unemployment and other indicators of a rising risk of recession are consistent with rate hikes working to slow demand, which will ultimately slow inflation.” The tough outlook was confirmed in S&P’s measure of manufacturing activity, which through November showed the largest fall in business activity in five years. The measure revealed a drop in employment and a broad reduction in new orders. Inflation pressures also fell. “The latest decline in demand reflected the impact of higher interest rates, while softening domestic and external conditions also contributed,” said Jingyi Pan, S&P Global Market Intelligence associate director. Queensland politicians are blaming each other for the crisis engulfing the state’s healthcare system, as paramedics say their concerns are not being taken seriously, and frontline workers report being too afraid of losing their jobs to speak out. Seven people have died while waiting for an ambulance since late June, including one Thornlands man who died during an 18-hour wait after calling Triple Zero. Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington was grilled over the pressures facing the system on Monday, as reporters asked why Health Minister Tim Nicholls had not faced media. Hospitals ramped at Brisbane’s Prince Charles Hospital. Courtney Kruk Frecklington said Nicholls was “working very, very hard … given the state of the health system that we inherited”, pinning Queensland’s crisis on failures of the former Labor government.

Advertisement

“What we are seeing is the work of that health crisis given to us by the former Labor government … that is why we have a bed shortage crisis,” she said. Related Article Queensland government Queensland can trust Triple Zero despite deaths waiting for ambulances: minister In parliament last week, Nicholls faced a barrage of questions about the Queensland Ambulance Service’s performance. After an emergency meeting with the premier, Queensland Health director-general and QAS commissioner on Wednesday, he briefly addressed media on Thursday afternoon, holding a prop folder labelled “Labor’s hospital failures”. “I think that the community can have confidence in Triple Zero, and they can have confidence in the paramedics and … the system,” he said.

Advertisement

“Because we’ve got a plan. We’re not dodging responsibility. We’re accepting responsibility for fixing the mess that’s been left to us by Labor.” Opposition Leader Steven Miles hit back on Monday, saying the LNP was not taking accountability. “This shouldn’t be a test of our front line,” Miles said. “It should be a test of Tim Nicholls and his leadership, and he should tell Queenslanders today what’s happening in the health system and what he’s doing about it.”

Advertisement

Miles said problems with response wait times, hospital ramping and bed shortages could be traced back to decisions made in the last two years. Related Article Emergency services Family speaks out after man dies waiting 18 hours for ambulance “I think Queenslanders understand that the health system goes through periods of demand. I don’t think they realise that this government hadn’t budgeted to account for that demand. “These issues are far, far worse than they were in 2024.” Queensland Hospital Watch co-founder Rosemary Wanless said she had heard from concerned nurses and paramedics before recent patient deaths made headlines, and slammed Nicholls for his “political stunt” last week.

Advertisement

“He could have pulled his head in and actually taken this seriously and been professional in that moment,” Wanless said. “[This government] is choosing to ostrich their heads in the sand than acknowledge the problem.” Wanless shared messages from frontline workers, including one that said paramedics were being forced into dangerous decisions to move patients into emergency departments. Another said frontline workers were too afraid of losing their jobs to speak out. “QAS staff are told from day one that they’re not to speak publicly about these issues,” they wrote.

“But how can a service that all of our own loved ones rely on not be up for public scrutiny? People should be able to raise concerns without risking their jobs.” QAS has been contacted for comment. The United Workers Union, which covers paramedics, said the issue was the handover to hospitals. “QAS has put supervisors on ramps for past weeks to help facilitate the movement of patients,” said Queensland secretary Fiona Scalon. “That can only do so much because the issue is inside the hospitals. In today’s AFL briefing: Swans stars Heeney and Warner return from banishment

A Shepparton ruckman was the first of nine players selected in the AFL rookie draft

Hawks recruits hit the track as focus turns to body language Pullman quartet return to track alongside Papley Jonathan Drennan Sydney Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon trained officially with the club for the first time on Monday since being cleared, along with North Melbourne recruit Nick Blakey, of criminal conduct by Victoria Police after a night of partying at the Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Isaac Heeney arrives at Bat and Ball Oval with teammates for first day of pre-season. Janie Barrett

Advertisement

Tom Papley also trained with the squad for the first time since the AFL suspended him for the first three games of the 2027 season after police caught him driving with cocaine and MDMA in his system earlier this month. Papley has been summoned to appear before Waverley Local Court this Thursday. Papley’s suspension is the strongest penalty imposed on a player caught on a public drugs matter. Chad Warner at training on Monday morning. Janie Barrett The Swans banned the “Pullman Five” for the remainder of the season in August for breaching the club’s behavioural standards, and were also barred from All-Australian honours. Speaking to this masthead, Warner said he was looking forward to repaying the faith of his teammates during his suspension.

Advertisement

“We’ve been training with everyone probably for a couple of months now over at Centennial [Park],” Warner said. “Everyone’s getting back in the groove, gelling, and I can’t wait [for pre-season], to be honest. “The boys have been great, and I think from the start they’ve all just wanted to do what they can, really. Tom Papley at the Swans firs pre-season training session on Monday. Janie Barrett “There’s obviously a lot of things people can’t do as well, so everyone’s in a tough position, but I think that’s the best thing about mates and teammates like this – they’re always going to have your back.” Bice, Jordon, Heeney and Warner are all free to play in the round one clash against Geelong at the SCG on March 17.

Advertisement

Warner arrived early to training to complete running drills on the oval that is commonly used for community football, while Papley arrived with a heavily strapped right knee and left the session early. Blakey began training with North Melbourne on November 9, joining the club’s first- to fourth-year players who started pre-season earlier than the Swans because they did not qualify for the finals. Loading Warner and Heeney trained with senior teammates in an unofficial session at Centennial Park last week. Monday was the first day of official pre-season for first- to fourth-year players. The rest of the Swans senior players including Charlie Curnow, James Rowbottom and Brodie Grundy will return to training next Monday.

AFL 2026 The AFL has an equalisation problem. This is what it has to do next Michael Gleeson Sports columnist Asked last week about the reintegration of Heeney, Warner and Jordon into the club, Swans AFLW star Chloe Molloy said her primary concern was ensuring the culture of her squad was protected. “I have no idea [how reintegrating Heeney, Warner, Jordon will go],” Molloy said. “All I know is there is a culture within the [AFL]W program that I want to nurture and be a part of.”

Essendon build ruck depth as host of players earn another chance Marc McGowan A 207-centimetre ruckman from Shepparton was the first of nine players selected in the AFL rookie draft on Monday who were not on a list this year. Essendon added Boston Dowling out of their VFL program with the No.1 pick in the rookie draft to provide more ruck depth behind Nick Bryan, Vigo Visentini and makeshift options Peter Wright and Lachie Blakiston. The 21-year-old trained with Richmond last summer but missed out on a pre-season supplemental selection period spot before impressing for the Bombers’ VFL team this year to finally earn his shot.

Western Jet Jacob Marron (GWS), Dandenong Stingrays’ Marcus Prasad (Carlton), Gippsland Power’s Cody Templeton (Adelaide), Northern Knights’ Max Downes (Geelong) and Kai Parker (Brisbane), Calder Cannon Charlie Robbins (Geelong) and Sandringham Dragons’ Albert MacGowan (Hawthorn) are also first-time draftees. Boston Dowling. Essendon Football Club MacGowan, a consistent midfielder who won the two-kilometre time trial at the draft combine in five minutes and 59 seconds, was one of the unluckiest players not to find an AFL home in the national draft last week. He won the Dragons’ best-and-fairest award while averaging 28 disposals and five clearances. Templeton kicked five goals and was best afield in the Power’s Talent League grand final win over goalsneak Prasad’s Stingrays in September. Kallan Dawson returns to the AFL with the Giants after spending three-and-a-half seasons with North Melbourne, who originally picked him out of the 2022 mid-season rookie draft.

Dawson, 28, was a key defender at the Kangaroos, but reinvented himself as a forward at Williamstown this year, kicking 35 goals in 20 games. Eight further players were redrafted to the clubs that delisted them: Steely Green (Richmond), Dan Butler and Ryan Byrnes (St Kilda), Harry DeMattia (Collingwood), Riley Garcia (Western Bulldogs), Jaren Carr (Fremantle), and Koby Evans and Luke Lloyd (Brisbane). Harry DeMattia training with the Magpies in late 2023. The Bombers are set to sign ex-Docker Bailey Banfield and former Kangaroo Tyler Sellers, while the Crows will sign ex-Swan Harry Cunningham on a two-year deal.

Recruits on track as Hawks focus on body language Jon Pierik Hawthorn hope they can respond in the manner of their 2012 brethren, as fitness staff demanded strong body language after a gruelling running drill to finish the opening morning of official pre-season training. Back to business: Star forward Nick Watson was among the first-to-four-year players who officially returned to training on Monday. Getty Images While Monday technically was the return date for first-to-fourth-year players at the Hawks’ Dingley training base, there were several blue-chip stars who also took part in the intense two-hour session under a beating sun, complete with annoying flies.

Advertisement

The Hawks have redemption on their mind in 2027 after successive preliminary final defeats, the pain of which was similar to those who experienced the 2012 grand final loss to the Swans, this spurring a hat-trick of flags. David Hale, now the Hawks strategy and opposition coach, but a member of that ’12 team and of the ensuing three premiership sides, said he could sense the added drive this squad led by coach Sam Mitchell has. View post on X “Any time you get that close to what you want to do and succeed in, that motivation grows stronger. I was a part of a group in 2012 that was the same. You know, the next three years panned out well for us then,” Hale said. “This group, as well, wants to taste success. So, hopefully, setting a good foundation now will put them in a good position come that time of year [finals] again.”

High-profile recruits Ben King and Zach Merrett were among the big names who impressed, King working well inside 50m alongside Nick Watson. Fellow forwards Jack Gunston and Mabior Chol were not on the field, while Jack Ginnivan, Blake Hardwick and Tom Barrass are also not required to return to training until next week. Related Article Draft Luke Hodge’s son officially a Hawk; Drums and ‘duxes’ on frenetic AFL draft night An injury-free James Sicily moved well, while his co-captain Jai Newcombe ran laps for nearly an hour. Frankston defender Jackson Voss has been invited to train with the club in a bid to win a supplementary selection period list spot, while the small smattering of fans were delighted to watch Conor Nash after the Irishman’s season ended in August because of a neck injury, which required surgery. He recently returned home to be married, but has been working diligently over the off-season. “Yeah, he [Nash] has always been a very important player for the role that he plays, that big-bodied defensive mid who can put pressure on around the ball,” Hale said.

Advertisement

“Obviously, the [Cam] McKenzie and [Josh] Ward types we saw flourish in the back end of last year in his absence, but he’s a quality player, and we know what he can bring when he’s up and going.” Draftees Cooper Hodge, the son of four-time premiership great Luke, and ruckman Benji van Rooyen, the younger brother of Melbourne star Jacob, also took to the track and showed glimpses of why they were highly-rated selections last week. Conor Nash trained well upon his return from neck surgery on Monday. Getty Images The Hawks worked through a series of drills on all aspects of their game, Hale expecting the league-wide trend towards greater scoring, including through more forward handballs or greater numbers at the contest, to continue next season. What is already clear is that the Hawks are a gifted running team, and will again look to use this to their advantage.

Advertisement

While general fitness and football fitness are crucial, coaches also want strong body language after completing gut-wrenching runs, the Hawks breaking into groups at the end of their session to complete a series of interval “aerobic power” lap running. Related Article AFL 2026 Your AFL club’s list is taking shape, but there could be some late plot twists yet “I’m not sure it’s better [Hawks’ fitness compared to rivals], but our running profile has always been something we’ve spoken about as a group. It can be an advantage, whether that’s at the end of the first quarter, the end of the last quarter,” Hale said. “So, against the best, you know, it might come down to, as you said, in the prelim finals in the last 30 seconds. So, that’s why they [players] run around ovals, and that’s why they have to keep a smile on their face at this time of year.” When players were allowed to briefly regain their breath after completing bursts of running, for instance, over four minutes, then three minutes, fitness coaches loudly reminded them about “body language” and to “stay up”, with few players collapsing to their haunches or bent over with hands on knees.

Hale said projecting an unrelenting image to opponents was important. “Yeah, it’s a battle within your own head, but it’s a battle within the group as well to make sure we keep pushing ourselves to get better,” Hale said. Former Hawthorn star Tom Mitchell sparked a furore this month when he criticised the West Coast Eagles for their poor body language after exhausted players crashed to the turf, having completed a gruelling series of sprints.
